MN202611_wr8dwo6tu.t:
Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee Jones

"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.

The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.

A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.

About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.

The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview House

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support .

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.

Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".

The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.

Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth"

Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.

But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.

He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."

Marketing images appeared to show Castleview House as newly refurbished with bright white interiors

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.

According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.

But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".

In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.

It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.

However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.

Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."

While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.

The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties.

"The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.

Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.

Mo (right) pictured with a friend who also lived in the same building, says his ceiling collapsed and was not fixed for months

He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.

Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.

Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.

Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".

He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.

Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.

Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".

It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.

Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".

In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats.

Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.

Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure".

"Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.

The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.

None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.

Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented.

"It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."

The BepiColombo mission will spend at least a year studying Mercury

After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.

Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.

These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."

The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury

The BepiColombo mission blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.

With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.

This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.

The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform an 11-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.

If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.

A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury

Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.

Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.

But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.

Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.

And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.

The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.

These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe

As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.

There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.

Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.

BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.

Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.

"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.

"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."

Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.

A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London

Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.

A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.

A European Space Agency (ESA) craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), will view the planet from a distance.

A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.

Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.

The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.

"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.

"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."

With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.

Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

Remember Monday used to say that representing the UK at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest was the "scariest" moment of their career.

But an upcoming album and UK tour will send the adrenaline soaring again, according to members Holly-Anne Hull, Charlotte Steele and Lauren Byrne.

"We still feel nerves like it all the time," Hull told BBC Introducing.

The vocal trio have recorded a new session for the programme, which was the first to play their music on the radio in 2019.

Seven years on, their credits include festivals, singles and the Eurovision final, where they came 19th out of 28 countries.

"We're always feeling nerves like it," Hull said.

"About a month later, we were performing at Wembley Stadium and we were like, 'I can't take it'," Byrne recalled.

"How can you possibly feel nerves like that again?"

"The coolest rock star story ever": Remember Monday meet McFly

The gig, in front of 80,000 people, led to a high-profile 2026 tour with pop-rock group McFly.

"Our dressing room was next to theirs at Wembley Stadium," Hull told presenter Steph Nieuwenhuys on BBC Introducing Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight.

"We just hit it off... We just toured the whole summer with them. Their crowds are crazy.

"It's scary being launched brand new into this industry without really knowing what we were doing.

"They've kind of taken us under their wing and been like: 'We'll look after you, you've got this.'"

Remember Monday's debut album, Can We Press Rewind?, is another "terrifying-slash-exciting" moment, according to Byrne.

Pre-released singles include the latest, Dream Cheat, a playful riff on the "relatable" experience of having a nightmare that a partner has been unfaithful.

BBC Introducing - Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight

The close-harmony trio met at The Sixth Form College in Farnborough, Hampshire.

Steele went on to be a founding member of performing arts sixth form Artemis College, in Bracknell, Berkshire, while all three have experience of performing in West End theatre shows.

Joseph Zada stars as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

It's been 14 years since the release of the first Hunger Games movie, which helped establish the careers of talented young actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler.

This latest instalment, prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping, looks to do the same with its leading trio: 21-year-old Joseph Zada, 20-year-old Mckenna Grace and 23-year-old Whitney Peak.

Sitting down with BBC News at the start of a gruelling press run, the group were buzzing with a mixture of anticipation, nerves and excitement ahead of the release of the much-talked-about film.

Zada, who is taking on his first major role as lead Haymitch Abernathy, said they had been "clinging together" and "using each other, making sure we all feel supported".

Grace is the most experienced of the three, having grown up as a child star with appearances in TV series The Handmaid's Tale, The Haunting of Hill House and two of the recent Ghostbusters films.

Even then, she said joining The Hunger Games franchise is "so nerve-racking", adding "I don't think anything can prepare you for working on it - this is nothing like anything I've experienced."

Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace play District 12 tributes Haymitch Abernathy and Maysilee Donner

Peak, who starred in Netflix's Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, jokes that she and Zada have sought out Grace every time they have felt "stuck or confused about what's happening" while promoting the film, and Zada says she has been a "mentor" to the new actors.

Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the series, which to date is one of the highest-grossing film franchises of all time, bringing in more than $3.3bn (£2.51bn) worldwide since 2012.

It is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film and is based on the 2025 book of the same name by author Suzanne Collins.

Zada takes on the role of a teenage Haymitch, who is played by Woody Harrelson in the original films - a District 12 tribute in the games, chosen alongside Grace's character Donner.

Peak plays Lenore Dove, Haymitch's girlfriend.

Whitney Peak stars as Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove, who is left behind in District 12 while he fights in the games

Reviews of the latest film have been generally positive, with several outlets praising Zada's performance, noting the difficulty of stepping into Harrelson's shoes.

Zada says he spent months "completely invested" in Harrelson's performances in the first four The Hunger Games films, "watching everything I could find and then making notes" which he used "as a base layer to colour with my own ideas".

He didn't meet the Oscar-nominated actor until halfway through filming, but says his advice was to watch two films - Cool Hand Luke and Harold and Maud, with the former "helping a lot to ground my performance" and the latter serving as "a fun watch".

Jesse Plemons, who plays a games producer in the film, told the BBC he knew Zada's role would be "a massive undertaking" after reading the script but says he was "amazed by his stamina and grace".

This was echoed by Glenn Close, who plays an over-the-top representative from the ruling Capitol, who said she "loved working with" Zada.

"When I met them [Zada, Grace and Peak] for the first time, they'd done all the games and been through it all.

"The first thing Joe said to me was 'I'm a bit traumatised' and he wasn't even done - there was still so much to go," she added.

Glenn Close plays an over-the-top government official from the Capitol in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

The film, which includes an ensemble cast of Ralph Fiennes, Maya Hawke, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning, is set during the 50th edition of The Hunger Games - with most elements of the brutal dystopian universe that fans have come to recognise from the previous films returning in this iteration.

Adapted from Collins' novels, the series is set in a post-apocalyptic North America, which is known as Panem, with the first trilogy focusing on a teenage Katniss Everdeen, who was played by Lawrence in the films.

Panem has 12 districts that participate in the yearly Hunger Games, produced and run by the governing area, the Capitol, as a punishment for rebellion.

Peak notes that being on set was an intense experience for the young cast and could "get overwhelming very quickly" on set, so they had to make sure to "keep it light between all the hard stuff".

"I don't think people realise how intensely bonding an experience like this is because we all spend days doing extremely physical and deeply emotional things," Grace says.

"It's like a little family on set; we've all been thankful to have each other," she added.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in cinemas now.

Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.

The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its £500m target.

In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures would be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.

The BBC welcomed the report, saying it had "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".

The NAO report , external also said the BBC's current measures were expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."

The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.

BBC director-general Matt Brittin previously described the licence fee model as a "busted flush"

The NAO found the BBC's licence fee income had fallen by 26% in real terms over the last decade, because in part of the significant changes in audience habits.

The proportion of UK adults using BBC television, iPlayer, radio or online services on an average week also fell from 90% in 2021-22 to 81% in 2025-26, the NAO said.

The report noted the corporation's public service broadcasting operating deficit had reached £209m in the last financial year.

The BBC has already announced plans to reduce spending by about 10%, including cuts to programming across its news, nations and content divisions.

Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank, Live At The Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and RuPaul's Drag Race UK are among the TV programmes to have been cut so far.

Radio programmes are also being dropped from the schedules, such as BBC Radio 4's You and Yours, and The World Tonight.

The corporation has also announced plans to close the linear broadcast services of BBC Radio 4 Extra, BBC Three and BBC Scotland, with the latter two becoming online-only services.

The NAO said the BBC expected to face difficult choices about the scale and scope of its services as part of its latest savings programme, with further content reductions expected to have a greater impact on audiences.

It warned the corporation was likely to find it harder to identify further savings following its previous cost-cutting programmes.

The NAO also found the broadcaster had not properly monitored the cumulative impact of its previous savings on audiences, service quality and organisational capability.

It also raised concerns about the BBC's risk management and governance arrangements, and said stronger oversight would be needed to deliver the more demanding savings programme.

In response to the report, the BBC said it welcomed the findings, adding that it had had to "make tough decisions due to sustained financial pressures driven by declining licence fee income, changing audience behaviour, increased competition and rising costs".

Berangere Michel, the BBC's group chief financial officer, said: "We welcome this report and are pleased that the NAO has acknowledged the significant savings already delivered by the BBC, with the programme on track to meet its target one year ahead of schedule.

"The BBC must respond to significant cost pressures while reinventing for a changing world. This continues to require tough decisions, while ensuring that the impacts on audiences and colleagues are minimised.

"We accept the NAO's recommendations and have already begun implementing them to strengthen the delivery of our current savings programme, while recognising there are further opportunities to build on this progress."

She added: "We will continue to engage with government to secure a new Charter that provides sufficient, sustainable and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come."
